title: USB Flashlight: Five LEDs on USB Power
description: Build the classic DIY USB flashlight from build-electronic-circuits.com: five LEDs, each with its own 100 Ω resistor, all side by side (in parallel) between the 5V and GND of a USB supply, with a slide switch to turn the light on and off. The Arduino's 5V and GND pins stand in for the USB breakout board, and a breadboard stands in for the perfboard. No program runs; the Arduino only supplies power.

steps.clip: Gather your Arduino Uno and USB cable, a breadboard, five LEDs, five 100 Ω resistors, a slide switch and some jumper wires. The Arduino's 5V and GND pins take the place of the USB breakout board.
Push the slide switch into the top half of the breadboard so its three legs sit in three side-by-side columns (for example columns 2, 3 and 4).
steps.goal: Seat the slide switch on the breadboard with each of its three legs in its own column.
hints: Each leg needs its own column, so the switch goes along the board, not across it.
Keep it in the top half, above the middle gap.

steps.clip: Run a red jumper wire from the Arduino's 5V pin to the column of the switch's middle leg.
steps.goal: Feed the USB 5V supply (the Arduino's 5V pin) into the switch's middle leg.
hints: The middle leg is the switch's common leg: it connects to one end leg or the other.
Use a free hole in the same column as the middle leg.

steps.clip: Take the first 100 Ω resistor. Push one leg (either one) into the red + line along the top edge of the breadboard, and the other leg into an empty column in the top half, e.g. column 8.
steps.goal: Place the first resistor between the + power line and an empty column.
hints: Resistors have no direction, so either leg can go in the + line.
The + line is the long strip marked with a red line and +.

steps.clip: Run a jumper wire from the column of one end leg of the switch (the leg next to the middle one) to the red + line. Now the switch decides whether 5V reaches the + line.
steps.goal: Connect one end leg of the switch to the + line that feeds the resistors.
hints: Leave the switch's third leg unconnected; only the middle leg and one end leg are used.
Use a free hole of the end leg's column.

steps.clip: Take the first LED. Put its long leg in the same column as the resistor's free leg, and its short leg into the blue − line along the top edge.
steps.goal: Connect the first LED's long leg (+) to the free end of its resistor, with the short leg on the − line.
hints: The long leg is the + side; the LED won't light if it's reversed.
The − line is the strip marked with a blue line and −.

steps.clip: Run a black jumper wire from the blue − line to a GND pin on the Arduino.
steps.goal: Connect the − line (the LEDs' short legs) to GND.
hints: Any GND pin on the Arduino works; they are all the same.
This is the USB supply's GND.

steps.clip: Take the second 100 Ω resistor. Push one leg into the red + line and the other leg into a new empty column in the top half, e.g. column 12.
steps.goal: Add a second resistor from the + line to its own empty column.
hints: Use a column no other part is in yet.
Either resistor leg can go in the + line.

steps.clip: Put the second LED's long leg in the same column as the second resistor's free leg, and its short leg in the blue − line.
steps.goal: Connect the second LED between its resistor and the − line, long leg toward the resistor.
hints: Long leg to the resistor, short leg to the − line.
Each LED + resistor pair sits side by side (in parallel) with the others.

steps.clip: Take the third 100 Ω resistor. Push one leg into the red + line and the other leg into a new empty column, e.g. column 16.
steps.goal: Add a third resistor from the + line to its own empty column.
hints: Use a column no other part is in yet.
Either resistor leg can go in the + line.

steps.clip: Put the third LED's long leg in the same column as the third resistor's free leg, and its short leg in the blue − line.
steps.goal: Connect the third LED between its resistor and the − line, long leg toward the resistor.
hints: Long leg to the resistor, short leg to the − line.

steps.clip: Take the fourth 100 Ω resistor. Push one leg into the red + line and the other leg into a new empty column, e.g. column 20.
steps.goal: Add a fourth resistor from the + line to its own empty column.
hints: Use a column no other part is in yet.
Either resistor leg can go in the + line.

steps.clip: Put the fourth LED's long leg in the same column as the fourth resistor's free leg, and its short leg in the blue − line.
steps.goal: Connect the fourth LED between its resistor and the − line, long leg toward the resistor.
hints: Long leg to the resistor, short leg to the − line.

steps.clip: Take the fifth 100 Ω resistor. Push one leg into the red + line and the other leg into a new empty column, e.g. column 24.
steps.goal: Add the fifth resistor from the + line to its own empty column.
hints: Use a column no other part is in yet.
Either resistor leg can go in the + line.

steps.clip: Put the fifth LED's long leg in the same column as the fifth resistor's free leg, and its short leg in the blue − line. Before plugging in USB, check that the + line and − line don't touch anywhere (the guide uses a multimeter continuity check).
steps.goal: Connect the last LED between its resistor and the − line, then make sure 5V is not shorted to GND.
hints: Long leg to the resistor, short leg to the − line.
No wire or leg should go straight from the + line to the − line.

steps.clip: Upload the empty sketch; the Arduino is only a USB power supply here. Slide the switch one way and all five LEDs light up, slide it back and they go off.

source.title: How To Build a USB Flashlight: A Simple DIY Tutorial

substitutions.why: The Arduino's 5V and GND pins stand in for the USB breakout — they are the USB port's 5V supply.
A breadboard stands in for the perfboard. To build it the guide's way, pick No breadboard → Solder on the level card.

substitutions.guide: 1× Switch (to turn the light ON and OFF)
substitutions.why: A slide switch, as the guide's on/off switch.

substitutions.guide: 1× USB power source (computer, wall adapter or power bank)
